title: Diamond Classification, Valuation, and Mining
content:
DIAMOND COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE:

CLASSIFICATION (4Cs):
1. Carat Weight: 1 carat = 0.2 grams. Price increases exponentially with size.
   - 0.5ct: $1,000-$5,000/ct (gem quality)
   - 1.0ct: $3,000-$15,000/ct
   - 2.0ct: $8,000-$50,000/ct
   - 5.0ct+: $20,000-$200,000+/ct

2. Color: D (colorless) to Z (light yellow/brown)
   - D-F: Colorless (premium, $10,000+/ct)
   - G-J: Near colorless ($5,000-$10,000/ct)
   - K-M: Faint color ($2,000-$5,000/ct)
   - Fancy colors: pink, blue, green, yellow — can exceed $1M/ct at auction

3. Clarity: FL (flawless) to I3 (included)
   - FL/IF: Flawless/Internally Flawless (rare, premium)
   - VVS1-VVS2: Very Very Slightly Included
   - VS1-VS2: Very Slightly Included
   - SI1-SI2: Slightly Included
   - I1-I3: Included (commercial grade)

4. Cut: Excellent to Poor
   - Round Brilliant: most popular, 57-58 facets
   - Fancy shapes: Princess, Emerald, Oval, Marquise, Pear, Cushion
   - Excellent cut: maximizes light return (brilliance + fire)

MINING METHODS:
1. Kimberlite Pipe Mining (primary deposits)
   - Open pit: stripping ratio 5-10:1
   - Underground: below 300m depth
   - Processing: Dense Media Separation (DMS) + X-ray sorting
   - Recovery: 1-2 carats per 100 tonnes ore (typical)

2. Alluvial Mining (secondary deposits)
   - Dredging river gravels
   - Excavation of terrace deposits
   - Processing: scrubbing + DMS
   - Recovery: 0.01-1.0 carats per m³ gravel

3. Marine Mining
   - Offshore deposits (Namibia, South Africa)
   - Vessels with seabed crawlers
   - Recovery: 1-5 carats per 100m³ seabed

GLOBAL PRODUCTION:
- Russia: 41M carats/year (largest by volume)
- Botswana: 23M carats/year (largest by value)
- DRC: 15M carats/year (industrial + gem)
- Australia: 13M carats/year (Argyle mine now closed)
- Canada: 16M carats/year
- South Africa: 8M carats/year
- Angola: 10M carats/year
- Tanzania: 2M carats/year
- Sierra Leone: 0.5M carats/year

PRICING BENCHMARKS:
- Bulk industrial: $5-$50/ct
- Gem quality melee (0.05-0.18ct): $200-$2,000/ct
- 1ct round D IF: $12,000-$25,000/ct
- Fancy vivid pink: $100,000-$2,000,000/ct
- Fancy vivid blue: $200,000-$4,000,000/ct

MARKET INTELLIGENCE:
- De Beers controls 30% of rough diamond supply
- Alrosa (Russia): 28% of global supply
- Rio Tinto: 12% (now mainly diamonds)
- Annual rough diamond market: $15-18 billion
- Polished diamond market: $28-32 billion
- Key trading centers: Antwerp, Mumbai, Tel Aviv, New York, Dubai

title: Ruby Classification, Origin, and Valuation
content:
RUBY COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE:

CLASSIFICATION:
- Color: The most important factor
  - Pigeon Blood Red: the finest (vivid red with slight blue undertone)
  - Vivid Red: premium quality
  - Deep Red: commercial to fine quality
  - Pinkish-Red: lighter, less valuable
  - Purplish-Red: lower value

- Clarity: Type I, II, III (different from diamonds)
  - Type I: typically eye-clean (Burmese rubies)
  - Type II: some inclusions expected (Thai rubies)
  - Type III: heavily included (some African rubies)

- Treatment: Heat treatment common and accepted
  - Unheated: premium (30-50% price premium)
  - Heat treated: standard (90% of market)
  - Lead glass filled: low quality, significant discount
  - Diffusion treated: disclosure required

ORIGINS AND VALUE:
1. Myanmar (Burma) — Pigeon Blood
   - Mogok Valley: world's finest rubies
   - Price: $50,000-$500,000/ct (pigeon blood)
   - Mining: artisanal in marble host rock

2. Mozambique — Montepuez
   - Discovery: 2009
   - Large deposits of fine quality
   - Price: $10,000-$100,000/ct
   - Production: 40% of global supply

3. Tanzania — Winza
   - Fine rubies in amphibolite host rock
   - Price: $5,000-$50,000/ct
   - Growing reputation

4. Madagascar
   - Andilamena and Vatomandry
   - Commercial to fine quality
   - Price: $1,000-$20,000/ct

5. Vietnam — Luc Yen
   - Marble-hosted rubies
   - Fine quality
   - Price: $5,000-$30,000/ct

AUCTION RECORDS:
- Sunrise Ruby (25.59ct,缅甸): $30.4 million (2015)
- Blood Royale Ruby (27.02ct): $34.8 million (2023)
- Estrela de Fura (55.22ct, Mozambique): $34.8 million (2023)

MINING METHODS:
- Open pit: weathered ruby-bearing marble
- Tunnel mining: following ruby veins
- Artisanal: hand tools, no explosives near gems
- Processing: hand sorting, no chemical treatment

MARKET:
- Annual ruby market: $3-4 billion
- Key trading: Thailand (Bangkok), Sri Lanka, India
- Growing demand from US, China, Middle East

title: Emerald Classification, Origin, and Valuation
content:
EMERALD COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE:

CLASSIFICATION:
- Color: The dominant value factor
  - Vivid Green: finest (strong green, not too dark)
  - Deep Green: fine quality
  - Medium Green: commercial quality
  - Light/Salty Green: lower value
  - Blue-Green: less valuable (more beryl than emerald)

- Clarity: Type III (inclusions expected and accepted)
  - Jardin: garden-like inclusions (French term, acceptable)
  - Fingerprint inclusions: common
  - Three-phase inclusions: diagnostic of origin
  - Eye-clean: rare and premium

- Treatment: Oil/resin filling standard
  - No oil: premium (50-100% price premium)
  - Minor oil: accepted
  - Moderate to significant oil: discount
  - Opticon/resin fill: significant discount

ORIGINS AND VALUE:
1. Colombia — Muzo, Coscuez, Chivor
   - World's finest emeralds
   - Color: vivid green with slight blue undertone
   - Price: $5,000-$100,000/ct (fine quality)
   - Production: 50% of global supply
   - Mining: underground in black shale host rock

2. Zambia — Kagem Mine
   - Second largest producer
   - Color: deep green, slightly bluish
   - Price: $3,000-$50,000/ct
   - Production: 20% of global supply

3. Brazil — Minas Gerais
   - Commercial to fine quality
   - Price: $1,000-$20,000/ct
   - Large volume production

4. Colombia — Coscuez
   - High quality
   - Price: $5,000-$80,000/ct

5. East Africa — Tanzania, Madagascar, Mozambique
   - Emerging sources
   - Commercial to fine quality
   - Price: $1,000-$15,000/ct

AUCTION RECORDS:
- Rockefeller Emerald (18.04ct, Colombia): $5.5 million (2017)
- Sakura Emerald (21.84ct): $1.3 million (2021)

MARKET:
- Annual emerald market: $2-3 billion
- Key trading: Bogota (Colombia), Mumbai, Antwerp
- Growing demand from Asian markets
- Lab-grown emeralds: growing but separate market

title: Tanzanite: The World's Rarest Gem
content:
TANZANITE COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE:

UNIQUE FACTS:
- Found ONLY in Merelani Hills, Arusha, Tanzania (20km long deposit)
- Discovered: 1967 by Manuel d'Souza
- A variety of the mineral zoisite
- 1,000 times rarer than diamond
- Predicted to be exhausted within 20-30 years

CLASSIFICATION:
- Color: Blue to violet-blue (trichroic: blue, violet, burgundy)
  - AAA (Vivid): strongest blue with violet flash — premium
  - AA: medium blue-violet — fine quality
  - A: lighter blue-violet — commercial
  - B/C: brownish or grayish — low quality

- Treatments: Heat treatment standard and accepted
  - Converts brownish zoisite to blue tanzanite
  - 99% of tanzanite is heat treated
  - Unheated tanzanite: rare and premium

- Size: larger sizes more available than other gems
  - 5-10ct: common
  - 20-50ct: available
  - 100ct+: museum quality

PRICING:
- 1ct AAA: $800-$2,000/ct
- 5ct AAA: $1,500-$4,000/ct
- 10ct AAA: $2,500-$6,000/ct
- 50ct+ AAA: $4,000-$10,000/ct
- Unheated AAA: 30-50% premium above

MINING:
- Open pit: 0-60m depth (blocks A and B)
- Underground: 60-400m depth (blocks C and D)
- Block C: deepest, highest quality
- Artisanal mining: thousands of small-scale miners
- Large-scale: TanzaniteOne (now TanzaniteOne Mining)

MARKET:
- Annual production: 2,000-3,000 kg
- Total known reserves: >150 million carats
- Annual market value: $500 million-$1 billion
- Key trading: Arusha (local), Antwerp, Mumbai
- Investment potential: increasing as mine depletes

INVESTMENT CONSIDERATIONS:
- Price has increased 20x since 2000
- Scarcity driving long-term value appreciation
- Certified stones (TanzaniteOne or GIA) command premium
- Synthetic tanzanite exists but is distinguishable
- Buy only from reputable dealers with certificates

title: Tsavorite: East Africa's Green Gold
content:
TSAVORITE COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE:

OVERVIEW:
- A green variety of grossular garnet
- Discovered: 1967 by Campbell Bridges in Kenya/Tanzania border
- Named after Tsavo National Park, Kenya
- Found in metamorphic schist deposits
- Rarer than emerald and often more brilliant

CLASSIFICATION:
- Color: Vivid green (chromium-traced)
  - AAA: deep vivid green, no brown — premium
  - AA: medium green — fine quality
  - A: light green — commercial
  - Low: brownish green — low value

- Clarity: typically eye-clean (better than emerald)
- Hardness: 7-7.5 (more durable than emerald)

ORIGINS AND VALUE:
1. Kenya — Voi, Taita-Taveta County
   - World's original tsavorite deposit
   - Grades: 0.5-5.0 g/t in schist host rock
   - Price: $500-$5,000/ct (fine quality)

2. Tanzania — Merelani Hills, Simanjiro
   - Extension of Kenyan deposits
   - Fine quality
   - Price: $500-$4,000/ct

3. Madagascar
   - Emerging deposits
   - Commercial quality
   - Price: $200-$2,000/ct

4. Pakistan/Afghanistan
   - Small production
   - Fine quality
   - Price: $300-$3,000/ct

MARKET:
- Annual production: <50,000 carats (very limited)
- Annual market: $20-50 million
- Price increasing as mines deplete
- Investment potential: high (scarcity)
- No synthetic tsavorite on market

MINING:
- Open cast and tunnel mining
- Hand tools near gem zones
- Processing: manual sorting and grading
- Production limited by small deposit sizes
